name: circular-list
summary: Builds a list whose last pair points back at the first, so walking it never ends.
explanation: Every ordinary list ends. Its last cdr is the empty list, and that is the signal to stop. circular-list builds the one kind of list that does not: it conses the arguments in order and then makes the final cdr point back at the head, so the chain closes into a ring. Walking it with car and cdr yields the arguments over and over, forever, with no allocation past the initial cons cells. That makes it the natural representation for anything that repeats by nature -- turn order, a traffic light, a colour palette, the alternating signs in a series -- because the repetition lives in the data structure instead of in modular arithmetic scattered through the code. The cost is that every verb which walks to the end is now a hang, and the ones that are careful enough to detect the cycle report failure instead. You do not iterate a circular list; you take from it, and you decide when to stop.

examples.code:
(define (take-from c n)
  (if (= n 0) '() (cons (car c) (take-from (cdr c) (- n 1)))))
(display (take-from (circular-list 1 2 3) 8))
(newline)
examples.note: (1 2 3 1 2 3 1 2) -- three elements, eight taken, and the ring supplied the difference.
(circular? #t proper? #f length+ #f) -- it is a list by every structural test except the one that matters to a loop.

examples.code:
(define (nth-of c n) (if (= n 0) (car c) (nth-of (cdr c) (- n 1))))
(define seats (circular-list 'north 'east 'south 'west))
(display (map (lambda (turn) (nth-of seats turn)) '(0 1 2 3 4 5 9)))
(newline)
examples.note: (north east south west north east east) -- turn 9 is turn 1 again, and no modulo appears anywhere in the code.

caveats: Never hand one to display, length, list-ref, list-tail, map, or reverse. Verbs that check will raise; verbs that do not will hang or exhaust memory.
With no arguments it returns the empty list, which is proper, not circular. (circular-list? (circular-list)) is #f.
The recursion that consumes it must be bounded by a counter or a predicate you supply. There is no end to detect.
It shares structure with itself by construction: for a one-element ring, (eq? c (cdr c)) is #t. Mutating any pair changes every future pass over it.
circular-list? costs a walk with cycle detection. It is a diagnostic, not something to call inside a loop over the same list.
usecases: Turn order in a game, where play returns to the first player without any wraparound arithmetic.
A repeating palette, texture, or waveform sampled at an arbitrary number of steps.
Round-robin assignment of work to a fixed pool of workers.

learn.concept: A cycle in the data replaces modular arithmetic in the code -- and takes termination with it.
learn.progression: Build a three-element ring and take eight from it. Then try to display it and watch it fail, and understand why: every list verb you know is written around a last cdr that is not there. Then write your own bounded take, and you have the only interface a circular list ever offers.

row-2-audit.eng-program:
(define (turn-order players rounds)
  (let loop ((c (apply circular-list players)) (n (* rounds (length players))) (out '()))
    (if (= n 0) (reverse out) (loop (cdr c) (- n 1) (cons (car c) out)))))
(display (list 'one (turn-order '(ann bo cy) 1)
               'two (turn-order '(ann bo cy) 2)
               'solo (turn-order '(ann) 3)))
(newline)
row-2-audit.math-program:
(define (alternating-sum terms)
  (let loop ((c (circular-list 1 -1)) (rest terms) (acc 0))
    (if (null? rest) acc (loop (cdr c) (cdr rest) (+ acc (* (car c) (car rest)))))))
(display (map alternating-sum '((1 2 3 4) (5 5 5) (10))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.cs-program:
(define (steps-to-return elems)
  (let ((start (apply circular-list elems)))
    (let loop ((p (cdr start)) (n 1))
      (if (eq? p start) n (loop (cdr p) (+ n 1))))))
(display (map steps-to-return '((a) (a b) (a b c d))))
(newline)
row-2-audit.problem: A scheduler needs the next player, forever, from a fixed roster. Candidates: circular-list (the wraparound is structural, the loop just cdrs, and nothing computes an index), a vector plus (modulo i n) (works, but the modulo has to be right at every call site and the roster length has to travel with it), list-tabulate over a repeated pattern (materialises the whole schedule up front, so the number of rounds must be known before the first turn), an infinite stream of promises (correct and lazier, but pays a force per turn for repetition that is not actually lazy). circular-list wins because the repetition is a property of the roster, not of the caller.
row-2-audit.explanation: eng: a turn generator called for one round, two rounds, and a one-player roster where every turn is the same person. math: an alternating-sign sum where the +1/-1 ring pairs off against the terms and simply stops when the terms do, over three series of different parity. cs: measuring the cycle length by walking until a pair is eq? to the head, which recovers the argument count from the ring itself for rings of size 1, 2, and 4.
row-2-audit.meta: Notice the eng and math programs never ask how long the ring is. The ring is the shorter argument in the math case and the loop is bounded by the other one, which is exactly the discipline a circular list demands: something else must own termination.
row-2-audit.eng: Turn order that wraps by arithmetic breaks the day someone adds a player and forgets a modulo. Turn order that wraps by structure cannot.
row-2-audit.math: An alternating series is a pointwise product with the two-cycle (1 -1). Writing it that way makes the sign pattern data rather than a parity test on the index.
row-2-audit.cs: eq? against the head is the cheapest cycle probe there is when you already hold the entry pair -- no tortoise, no hare, no marking.

row-3-dimension.setup: Something that repeats forever, sampled for as long as the caller cares to sample it.

rungs.code:
(define (take-from c n) (if (= n 0) '() (cons (car c) (take-from (cdr c) (- n 1)))))
(display (list (take-from (circular-list 1 2 3) 7)
               (take-from (circular-list 0) 4)
               (take-from (circular-list 2 4) 5)))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a traffic light stepped through a shift, where the phase durations differ
rungs.code:
(define (signal-at-second s)
  (let loop ((c (circular-list '(red . 30) '(green . 25) '(amber . 5))) (t s))
    (if (< t (cdar c)) (caar c) (loop (cdr c) (- t (cdar c))))))
(display (map signal-at-second '(0 29 30 54 55 59 60 100)))
(newline)

rungs.domain: a dispatcher spreading a queue of jobs over a fixed pool of workers
rungs.code:
(define (assign jobs workers)
  (let loop ((c (apply circular-list workers)) (j jobs) (out '()))
    (if (null? j)
        (reverse out)
        (loop (cdr c) (cdr j) (cons (cons (car j) (car c)) out)))))
(define plan (assign '(scan index thumb ocr pack) '(w1 w2)))
(display (list 'plan plan
               'w1-load (length (filter (lambda (p) (eq? (cdr p) 'w1)) plan))))
(newline)

row-3-dimension.explanation: On bare numbers the ring is just a repeating source and the only question is how many to take. On a traffic light the ring carries durations, so consumption is no longer one element per step -- the loop subtracts each phase's length from the clock and only advances when it runs out, which is a different traversal entirely. In the dispatcher the ring is not being sampled at all: it is being zipped against a finite queue, and the ring's job is to make the shorter sequence the one that decides when to stop. Same constructor; the ring goes from source, to clock, to pairing partner.
row-3-dimension.meta: The three rungs stop for three different reasons -- a counter, a running subtraction, and the exhaustion of an unrelated list. That is the whole design space for consuming a circular list, because it can never stop on its own.
row-3-dimension.eng: Phase timing that walks a ring of (colour . seconds) pairs handles unequal phases for free; a modulo over a fixed step size does not.
row-3-dimension.math: Sampling a periodic sequence at arbitrary t is a division into the period, and the loop here is that division carried out by repeated subtraction.
row-3-dimension.cs: Round-robin is a zip between an infinite sequence and a finite one. Once you see that, the load balance falls out of the queue length and the pool size with no bookkeeping.

row-4-proof.eng-program:
(define (nth-of c n) (if (= n 0) (car c) (nth-of (cdr c) (- n 1))))
(define (wraps-correctly? elems k)
  (let ((c (apply circular-list elems)) (len (length elems)))
    (equal? (nth-of c k) (list-ref elems (modulo k len)))))
(display (map (lambda (p) (wraps-correctly? (car p) (cdr p)))
              '(((a b c) . 0) ((a b c) . 4) ((a b c) . 30) ((z) . 7) ((a b) . 1))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.math-program:
(define (shape-is-exclusive? elems)
  (let ((c (apply circular-list elems)))
    (and (circular-list? c)
         (not (proper-list? c))
         (not (dotted-list? c))
         (not (length+ c))
         (= (length elems) (length elems)))))
(display (map shape-is-exclusive? '((1) (1 2) (1 2 3 4 5) (a b) (#f #f))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.cs-program:
(define (closes-at-its-own-length? elems)
  (let ((start (apply circular-list elems)))
    (let loop ((p (cdr start)) (n 1))
      (cond ((eq? p start) (= n (length elems)))
            ((> n 50) #f)
            (else (loop (cdr p) (+ n 1)))))))
(display (map closes-at-its-own-length? '((a) (a b) (a b c) (a a a) (1 2 3 4 5 6))))
(newline)
row-4-proof.claim: The element reached after k steps is the element at index k modulo the argument count; a circular list is circular and nothing else; and the ring closes after exactly as many pairs as there were arguments -- including when the arguments repeat.
row-4-proof.invariant: For all non-empty argument lists e and all k >= 0, nth(circular-list(e...), k) = e[k mod |e|]; circular-list?(c) and not proper-list?(c) and not dotted-list?(c) and length+(c) = #f; and the least n > 0 with cdr^n(c) eq? c is |e|
row-4-proof.meta: Three independent claims: the indexing law, the shape classification, and the cycle length. What would falsify them: an off-by-one at the join so that k = |e| landed on the second element, a ring that also answered #t to dotted-list?, or a constructor that collapsed duplicate arguments and closed early. The (a a a) case exists precisely to test that last one -- eq?-identical elements must still produce three distinct pairs.
row-4-proof.eng: The modulo law is the contract every caller assumes silently. Stating it is what lets you delete the modulo from their code.
row-4-proof.math: Exactly one of circular, proper, and dotted holds for any object. A constructor that broke the partition would break every dispatch written on it.
row-4-proof.cs: Cycle length equal to argument count is the claim that the constructor allocated one pair per argument and joined once. Duplicate arguments are the case where a sharing optimisation would show up as a shorter cycle.

row-5-emergence.eng-composition:
(define (cycle-source elems) (apply circular-list elems))
(define (stripe rows palette)
  (let loop ((c (cycle-source palette)) (r rows) (out '()))
    (if (null? r)
        (reverse out)
        (loop (cdr c) (cdr r) (cons (list (car r) (car c)) out)))))
(display (stripe '(head r1 r2 r3 r4) '(pale dark)))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.math-composition:
(define (sign-ring) (circular-list 1 -1))
(define (leibniz-terms n)
  (let loop ((c (sign-ring)) (k 0) (out '()))
    (if (= k n)
        (reverse out)
        (loop (cdr c) (+ k 1) (cons (* (car c) (/ 1 (+ (* 2 k) 1))) out)))))
(display (list 'terms (leibniz-terms 5) 'sum (apply + (leibniz-terms 6))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.cs-composition:
(define (pool workers) (apply circular-list workers))
(define (schedule jobs workers)
  (let loop ((c (pool workers)) (j jobs) (acc '()))
    (if (null? j)
        acc
        (loop (cdr c) (cdr j)
              (let ((w (car c)))
                (cons (cons w (+ 1 (or (cdr (or (assq w acc) '(x . 0))) 0))) 
                      (remove (lambda (p) (eq? (car p) w)) acc)))))))
(define load (schedule '(a b c d e f g) '(x y z)))
(display (list 'balanced (map (lambda (w) (cdr (assq w load))) '(x y z))
               'total (apply + (map cdr load))))
(newline)
row-5-emergence.base: circular-list makes a sequence that repeats forever with no end to detect.
row-5-emergence.emergent: eng: cycle-source is one call; stripe zips it against a finite list of rows, and alternating table shading falls out with no row index and no parity test -- change the palette to three colours and nothing else changes. math: sign-ring is one call; leibniz-terms builds the alternating odd-reciprocal series on top of it, so the sign pattern and the term formula stay separate and either can be swapped alone. cs: pool is one call; schedule walks it against a job queue while tallying, producing a load table that is provably balanced to within one job without ever computing (modulo i n).
row-5-emergence.meta: All three compositions are the same shape: the infinite thing supplies values, the finite thing supplies termination. The helper exists to hide the apply, and every caller above is written as if the ring were an ordinary list -- which it safely is, so long as the other argument runs out first.
row-5-emergence.eng: Zebra striping, tick marks, and repeating textures are all the same zip. Doing it with a ring means the pattern length is data and the loop never learns it.
row-5-emergence.math: Separating the sign sequence from the magnitude sequence is how alternating series get generalised: replace the two-cycle with any period and the same loop computes a different family.
row-5-emergence.cs: Round-robin balance to within one is a consequence of the pigeonhole principle applied to a zip, not something the scheduler has to enforce.
